newsitem.title: FRANCE: French right walks out of "henhouse" assembly.
newsitem.headline: French right walks out of "henhouse" assembly.

text.p: Right-wing deputies in the French National Assembly banged their desks in impotent rage when they were called naughty students on Tuesday, but when they were compared with noisy chickens, they walked out.

The new left-wing government faced a baptism of fire from heckling conservatives, stung by their general election debacle, in the first parliamentary televised question since it took office three weeks ago.

The conservatives, who lost power and more than half of their seats in the June 1 election, booed and banged on their desks as Socialist ministers tried to explain how they would reconcile budget restraints and new social measures.
Ministers with parliamentary experience were unmoved, knowing that he who has the microphone has the commanding voice.

Employment Minister Martine Aubry, under attack for her pledge to curb family benefits for the wealthy, responded by aggressively challenging protesters to dare convince millions of poor people that the money should be going to the rich.
But novice ministers faltered, stopping to try make sense of the heckling, or letting their voice be drowned in the din.
Foreign Minister Hubert Vedrine, a newcomer to parliament, apologised for his hoarse voice, saying he was a victim of air conditioning at last weekend's Group of Seven summit in Denver.

Education Minister Claude Allegre, a science professor making his Assembly debut, made the fatal mistake of stopping to listen to the hecklers. "I am used to speaking to students, who listen," he said. The interjections only increased.

Interior Minister Jean-Pierre Chevenement drew an outburst of abuse as he explained plans to give residence permits to thousands of immigrants in legal limbo, partially undoing the former conservative government's immigration crackdown.

The mood recalled the last weeks of a weakened Socialist government hounded out of office by the conservatives in 1993 rather than the first days of a new majority still enjoying a honeymoon with public opinion.
Then came ecologist Noel Mamere, a former television newscaster and ecologist member of the left-wing coalition.
"As a new parliamentarian, I am appalled by the attitude of this Assembly," he said. "I am not surprised French people feel increasingly remote from politicians when they see how we behave."
Singling out former security minister Robert Pandraud among the right-wing hecklers, he said: "Mr Pandraud spoke of a henhouse atmosphere, indeed he is used to addressing chickens."
Chicken is the French slang for police.

Indignant right-wingers trooped out of the chamber in protest as Socialist speaker Laurent Fabius tried to restore order, telling Mamere: "We must not attack each other. Question time is to ask questions."
Pandraud returned unrepentant and was allowed to make a brief statement defending the honour of the police.
